<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Predict to Skip: Linear Multistep Feature Forecasting for Efficient Diffusion Transformers</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">

</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">

</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Diffusion Transformers (DiT) have emerged as a widely adopted backbone for high-fidelity image and video generation, yet their iterative denoising process incurs high computational costs. Existing training-free acceleration methods rely on feature caching and reuse under the assumption of temporal stability. However, reusing features for multiple steps may lead to latent drift and visual degradation. We observe that model outputs evolve smoothly along much of the diffusion trajectory, enabling principled predictions rather than naive reuse. Based on this insight, we propose <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">PrediT</span>, a training-free acceleration framework that formulates feature prediction as a linear multistep problem. We employ classical linear multistep methods to forecast future model outputs from historical information, combined with a corrector that activates in high-dynamics regions to prevent error accumulation. A dynamic step modulation mechanism adaptively adjusts the prediction horizon by monitoring the feature change rate. Together, these components enable substantial acceleration while preserving generation fidelity. Extensive experiments validate that our method achieves up to <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="5.54\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5.54</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5.54\times</annotation></semantics></math> latency reduction across various DiT-based image and video generation models, while incurring negligible quality degradation.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Machine Learning, ICML
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18093v1/teaser.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/451;" width="476" height="451" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Accelerating Diffusion Transformer inference across multiple models. PrediT achieves significant speedup on various DiT-based architectures for both image and video generation while preserving visual quality.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Generative AI has achieved remarkable success across a wide range of applications, such as image and video generation, and controllable content creation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fui-Hoon Nah et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cao et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Diffusion models (DMs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ho et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rombach et al., 2022</a>)</cite> generate data by learning to reverse a gradual noising process, becoming the foundation of these advances. Early DMs relied on U-Net <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Blattmann et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ramesh et al., 2022</a>)</cite> architectures, but the limited receptive field of convolutional networks makes it difficult to capture long-range dependencies, restricting generation quality for complex scenes. Diffusion Transformers (DiT) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peebles and Xie, 2023</a>)</cite> have been proposed to address this limitation, leveraging the self-attention mechanism to model global relationships across the entire latent space. DiT models are now a widely adopted backbone behind state-of-the-art models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2023b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Esser et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
However, DiT inference is computationally expensive, as the quadratic attention cost combined with iterative denoising results in significant latency, making real-time generation impractical.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To accelerate DiT inference, two main categories of methods have been explored. Training-based approaches, such as distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Salimans and Ho, 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Meng et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and quantization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, reduce model complexity but require substantial training data and compute, and may degrade generation quality due to distribution shift. Training-free methods are increasingly popular due to their plug-and-play nature. Among these, caching-based approaches exploit the temporal redundancy in diffusion sampling by caching intermediate features and reusing them across consecutive steps, thereby reducing the number of full model samplings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Despite their efficiency, existing caching methods face limitations. Reuse-based methods such as DeepCache <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, FORA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Selvaraju et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and <math id="S1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math>-DiT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024c</a>)</cite> directly substitute previous model outputs for current ones, assuming that features remain unchanged across steps. However, this assumption breaks down in regions of high-dynamics along the denoising trajectory, leading to latent drift and potentially causing visual artifacts. To maintain acceptable quality, these methods must limit their acceleration ratio, resulting in modest speedups. More advanced approaches such as AB-Cache <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and TaylorSeer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025c</a>)</cite> extrapolate future features from historical information. While these methods improve upon naive reuse, they still suffer from error accumulation under fixed skip intervals, especially when the model output exhibits non-uniform dynamics.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">A key observation motivating our approach is that the model’s feature trajectory along the diffusion process is locally smooth (see <a href="#S1.F2.sf1" title="In Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Predict to Skip: Linear Multistep Feature Forecasting for Efficient Diffusion Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2(a)</span></a>), which suggests that the temporal structure of the denoising process can be exploited beyond naive reuse. To enable high-quality generation with aggressive acceleration, we identify two key challenges that must be addressed: <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(1) How to predict accurately and stably?</span> Naive reuse is a zero-order approximation, while existing forecasting methods rely on finite-difference estimation that is sensitive to noise and unstable in higher-order terms, causing error accumulation under large skip intervals. <span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(2) How to adapt the prediction horizon dynamically?</span> The dynamics varies significantly throughout the diffusion trajectory, with the initial and final phases exhibiting rapid changes while middle timesteps are smooth. A fixed skip schedule cannot account for this variation, leading to over-skipping (quality loss) or under-skipping (limited speedup).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we propose <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">PrediT</span> (<span id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pre</span>dictive <span id="S1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">DiT</span>), a training-free framework that treats feature estimation as a linear multistep prediction problem. We employ the Adams-Bashforth predictor, which directly combines historical function values without explicit derivative estimation, to extrapolate future model outputs with improved numerical stability. An Adams-Moulton corrector is further applied in high-dynamics regions to refine predictions and prevent error accumulation. A dynamic step modulation mechanism monitors the relative change rate and adaptively adjusts how many steps can be safely skipped. In contrast to prior methods that either passively reuse stale features or apply fixed-interval extrapolation without adaptive control, PrediT allows principled prediction with adaptive step modulation, achieving aggressive acceleration without quality degradation. As shown in <a href="#S1.F1" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ Predict to Skip: Linear Multistep Feature Forecasting for Efficient Diffusion Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, PrediT achieves <math id="S1.p5.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="4.28\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4.28</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4.28\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup on FLUX <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Labs et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, <math id="S1.p5.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2.48\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2.48</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.48\times</annotation></semantics></math> on DiT-XL/2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peebles and Xie, 2023</a>)</cite>, and <math id="S1.p5.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3.28\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.28</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.28\times</annotation></semantics></math> on HunyuanVideo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kong et al., 2024</a>)</cite> while maintaining comparable visual fidelity. In summary, our main contributions are:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We analyze why naive feature reuse leads to latent drift and show that diffusion trajectories are locally smooth, motivating higher-order polynomial prediction.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose PrediT, a training-free framework employing the Adams-Bashforth predictor with Adams-Moulton correction for stable feature forecasting. A dynamic step modulation mechanism monitors relative feature change rate and adaptively adjusts the prediction interval.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Extensive experiments on several DiT-based models demonstrate that PrediT achieves up to <math id="S1.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="5.54\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5.54</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5.54\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup while maintaining comparable generation quality, outperforming existing caching methods.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S1.F2.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18093v1/fig_v2_5.svg" id="S1.F2.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/300;" width="476" height="300"></object>

</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">

</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S1.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Analysis of direct feature reuse limitations. (a) Feature trajectory visualization via PCA shows local smoothness along the diffusion process. (b) Comparison of per-step approximation error and accumulated drift: naive reuse incurs significant error accumulation, while higher-order prediction methods reduce drift.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Diffusion Models.</span>
Diffusion models (DMs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ho et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rombach et al., 2022</a>)</cite> have achieved remarkable success across diverse generative tasks.
These models generate high-quality samples by progressively denoising data through an iterative refinement process <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Croitoru et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. Early diffusion models predominantly relied on U-Net architectures but exhibited challenges in capturing long-range dependencies across spatial regions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2023a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>.
To address these limitations, Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peebles and Xie, 2023</a>)</cite> replace the U-Net backbone with a transformer-based architecture <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Blattmann et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ramesh et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. Despite their impressive generation quality and scalability advantages, DiTs suffer from higher inference latency compared to their predecessors.
This computational burden has motivated extensive research into accelerating DiT inference.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Efficient Diffusion Models.</span>
Numerous approaches have been proposed to accelerate diffusion models.
DDIM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al., 2020a</a>)</cite> introduces a non-Markovian formulation that allows deterministic sampling with significantly fewer steps.
Model complexity reduction methods primarily focus on distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Salimans and Ho, 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Meng et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and quantization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, which transfer knowledge to smaller models or reduce numerical precision respectively. However, these methods often introduce notable trade-offs. Large sampling reduction can compromise generation quality and diversity, distillation requires substantial computational resources and may be limited by teacher model performance, and extreme quantization can lead to noticeable degradation in visual fidelity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Diffusion Model Caching.</span>
Cache-based acceleration methods have emerged as a promising training-free paradigm that exploits temporal redundancy in the denoising process.
DeepCache <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> pioneers this approach by caching and reusing high-level features across adjacent denoising timesteps. <math id="S2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math>-DiT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024c</a>)</cite> introduces a DiT-specific caching mechanism that stores feature differences rather than raw outputs.
FORA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Selvaraju et al., 2024</a>)</cite> implements a static caching strategy with a fixed interval parameter.
More sophisticated approaches include PAB <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which applies different broadcast ranges for spatial, temporal, and cross-modal attention mechanisms.
TeaCache <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025a</a>)</cite> intelligently determines when to use cached results based on input similarity.
SmoothCache <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025d</a>)</cite> analyzes layer-wise representation errors from calibration data to adaptively determine caching intensity.
ProfilingDiT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2025a</a>)</cite> distinguishes foreground-focused and background-focused transformer blocks, selectively caching static background features.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">While these direct feature reuse methods show impressive acceleration,
they rely on features from previous timesteps that may not perfectly align with the current denoising stage, causing accumulated errors that manifest as artifacts or quality loss.
An alternative approach involves predicting future timestep features rather than directly reusing cached results.
TaylorSeer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025c</a>)</cite> employs Taylor series expansion to forecast features at future timesteps. AB-Cache <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> provides theoretical justification through the Adams-Bashforth numerical method, revealing a linear relationship between outputs of consecutive denoising steps.
ABM-Solver <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2025b</a>)</cite> extends this framework for inversion and editing tasks.
Yet these prediction-based methods adopt fixed skip intervals without adaptive control, leading to error accumulation when feature dynamics vary significantly across the diffusion trajectory.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Method</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present PrediT, a training-free acceleration framework for DiTs that formulates feature prediction as a linear multistep problem. We first analyze the limitations of existing reuse-based methods and the smoothness property of diffusion trajectories, then introduce our predictor-corrector scheme with dynamic step modulation.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18093v1/overview.png" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/92;" width="476" height="92" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S3.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Overview of the PrediT framework. PrediT formulates feature prediction as a linear multistep problem, using historical model outputs to extrapolate future features and reduce redundant model calls. The threshold <math id="S3.F3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> and correction ratio <math id="S3.F3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> control the selection between ABM for high-dynamics and AB for low-dynamics regions.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Preliminaries</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Diffusion Models.</span>
DMs generate data by learning to reverse a gradual noising process. Given clean data <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, a forward process progressively adds Gaussian noise over timesteps <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> to produce <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. The reverse process starts from pure noise <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)</annotation></semantics></math> and iteratively denoises to recover <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>. It can be formulated as solving an Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al., 2020a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al., 2020b</a>)</cite>:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{dx}{dt}=f_{\theta}(x_{t},t)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{dx}{dt}=f_{\theta}(x_{t},t),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> is the model’s velocity prediction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lipman et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. The solution is obtained by numerical integration from <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=1</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=0</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Diffusion Transformers.</span>
Diffusion Transformers (DiT) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peebles and Xie, 2023</a>)</cite> replace the U-Net backbone with a transformer architecture. The latent <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is patchified into tokens, processed through self-attention and MLP layers, and unpatchified back to latent dimensions. Each DiT block applies Adaptive Layer Normalization (AdaLN) conditioned on timestep <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h^{\prime}=\text{Attn}(\text{AdaLN}(h)),\quad h^{\prime\prime}=\text{MLP}(\text{AdaLN}(h^{\prime}))." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>Attn</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext>AdaLN</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>′′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>MLP</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext>AdaLN</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h^{\prime}=\text{Attn}(\text{AdaLN}(h)),\quad h^{\prime\prime}=\text{MLP}(\text{AdaLN}(h^{\prime})).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">While DiT achieves superior generation quality, the quadratic attention cost combined with dozens of iterative steps makes inference computationally expensive.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Feature Reuse.</span>
Current caching methods accelerate inference by reusing previous model outputs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024c</a>)</cite>. Given the current state <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{n}</annotation></semantics></math> at timestep <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{n}</annotation></semantics></math>, these methods approximate the model output as:</p>
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{f}_{n}\approx f_{n-k}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>≈</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{f}_{n}\approx f_{n-k},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{n-k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{n-k}</annotation></semantics></math> is a cached output from <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> steps earlier. This zero-order approximation assumes <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> remains constant, incurring a local truncation error (LTE) of <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(\Delta t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(\Delta t)</annotation></semantics></math>. This error accumulates over consecutive skips, causing latent drift and visual artifacts.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Linear Multistep Methods.</span>
Linear multistep methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hairer et al., 1993</a>; <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Butcher, 2016</a>)</cite> are classical numerical techniques for solving ODEs that use multiple previous function values to achieve higher-order accuracy. Starting from the integral form of <a href="#S3.E1" title="In 3.1 Preliminaries ‣ 3 Method ‣ Predict to Skip: Linear Multistep Feature Forecasting for Efficient Diffusion Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Equation</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>:</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{n+1}=x_{n}+\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n+1}}f(x(s),s)\,ds," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.055em">+</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></msubsup><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{n+1}=x_{n}+\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n+1}}f(x(s),s)\,ds,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.2" class="ltx_p">these methods approximate the integrand by a polynomial interpolating past values <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{f_{n},f_{n-1},\ldots\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{f_{n},f_{n-1},\ldots\}</annotation></semantics></math>, achieving LTE of <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(\Delta t^{k+1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(\Delta t^{k+1})</annotation></semantics></math> for order <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>. This provides a principled framework for predicting model outputs without explicit derivative estimation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>PrediT Framework</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As illustrated in <a href="#S3.F3" title="In 3 Method ‣ Predict to Skip: Linear Multistep Feature Forecasting for Efficient Diffusion Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, PrediT combines an Adams-Bashforth predictor with an Adams-Moulton corrector under dynamic step modulation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Adams-Bashforth Predictor.</span>
The Adams-Bashforth (AB) method is an explicit linear multistep method that extrapolates from historical function values <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2022a</a>)</cite>. For order <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>, the AB formula is:</p>
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{n+1}=x_{n}+\Delta t\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\beta_{j}f_{n-j}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><mrow><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{n+1}=x_{n}+\Delta t\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\beta_{j}f_{n-j},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> are coefficients derived from Lagrange interpolation (see <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Adams Method Coefficients ‣ Predict to Skip: Linear Multistep Feature Forecasting for Efficient Diffusion Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>). Specifically, for the second-order case (AB2):</p>
<table id="S3.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{n+1}=x_{n}+\frac{\Delta t}{2}(3f_{n}-f_{n-1})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{n+1}=x_{n}+\frac{\Delta t}{2}(3f_{n}-f_{n-1}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.3" class="ltx_p">which achieves LTE of <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(\Delta t^{3})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(\Delta t^{3})</annotation></semantics></math>, compared to <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(\Delta t^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(\Delta t^{2})</annotation></semantics></math> for Euler. Crucially, AB directly combines historical function values without explicit derivative estimation, avoiding the instability of finite-difference approaches.</p>
</div>

<p id="S3.T1.6" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left ltx_figure_panel"><math id="S3.T1.m57" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\dagger" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo mathsize="0.800em">†</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\dagger</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.T1.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;"> <span id="S3.T1.6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bold</span> indicates the best result, <span id="S3.T1.6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">underline</span> indicates the second best. The same applies to the following tables.</span></p></div></div>

<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Adams-Moulton Corrector.</span>
While AB is efficient, its explicit nature can accumulate errors in high-dynamics regions. The Adams-Moulton (AM) method is an implicit corrector that includes the future value <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{n+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{n+1}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{n+1}=x_{n}+\Delta t\sum_{j=-1}^{k-1}\gamma_{j}f_{n-j}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><mrow><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{n+1}=x_{n}+\Delta t\sum_{j=-1}^{k-1}\gamma_{j}f_{n-j},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma_{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>γ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma_{-1}</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{n+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{n+1}</annotation></semantics></math>. For the second-order case (AM2):</p>
<table id="S3.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{n+1}=x_{n}+\frac{\Delta t}{12}(5f_{n+1}+8f_{n}-f_{n-1})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mn>12</mn></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{n+1}=x_{n}+\frac{\Delta t}{12}(5f_{n+1}+8f_{n}-f_{n-1}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.3" class="ltx_p">Combining AB as predictor and AM as corrector yields the Adams-Bashforth-Moulton (ABM) scheme <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karras et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, which first predicts <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{x}_{n+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{x}_{n+1}</annotation></semantics></math> using AB, then evaluates <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{f}_{n+1}=f_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{n+1},t_{n+1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{f}_{n+1}=f_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{n+1},t_{n+1})</annotation></semantics></math>, and finally corrects using AM. While ABM achieves LTE of <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(\Delta t^{4})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(\Delta t^{4})</annotation></semantics></math> and improved stability, it requires one extra model call compared to AB alone. As shown in <a href="#S1.F2" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ Predict to Skip: Linear Multistep Feature Forecasting for Efficient Diffusion Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>(b), AB significantly reduces approximation error compared to naive reuse, and ABM further improves accuracy with lower accumulated drift.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To balance accuracy and efficiency, PrediT dynamically selects between AB and ABM based on the relative feature change rate:</p>
<table id="S3.E9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{n}=\frac{\|f_{n}-f_{n-1}\|_{1}}{\|f_{n}\|_{1}+\epsilon}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{n}=\frac{\|f_{n}-f_{n-1}\|_{1}}{\|f_{n}\|_{1}+\epsilon},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> is a small constant for numerical stability. ABM is applied in high-dynamics regions where accuracy is critical, while AB is used in smooth regions to maximize speedup.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Dynamic Step Modulation.</span>
As shown in <a href="#S3.F4.sf1" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 3.2 PrediT Framework ‣ 3 Method ‣ Predict to Skip: Linear Multistep Feature Forecasting for Efficient Diffusion Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4(a)</span></a>, the model’s feature dynamics vary significantly along the diffusion trajectory, with initial and final phases exhibiting rapid changes. <a href="#S3.F4.sf2" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 3.2 PrediT Framework ‣ 3 Method ‣ Predict to Skip: Linear Multistep Feature Forecasting for Efficient Diffusion Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4(b)</span></a> further reveals that skipping in high-dynamics regions incurs substantially larger feature deviation than in low-dynamics regions. Notably, even skipping multiple steps in smooth regions produces less error than a single skip in high-dynamics regions. Therefore, a fixed skip schedule cannot adapt to this variation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karras et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. We compute the adaptive skip interval from the dynamics metric <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{n}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J=\left\lfloor\frac{\tau}{(\delta_{n}+\epsilon)^{1/(p+1)}}\right\rfloor," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>⌊</mo><mfrac><mi>τ</mi><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup></mfrac><mo>⌋</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J=\left\lfloor\frac{\tau}{(\delta_{n}+\epsilon)^{1/(p+1)}}\right\rfloor,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(10)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p5.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> is the threshold parameter and <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> is the sensitivity exponent. The decision logic selects ABM without skipping when <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{n}\geq\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>≥</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{n}\geq\tau</annotation></semantics></math>, ABM with limited skipping when <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\cdot r\leq\delta_{n}&lt;\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\cdot r\leq\delta_{n}&lt;\tau</annotation></semantics></math>, and AB only with large skipping when <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{n}&lt;\tau\cdot r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{n}&lt;\tau\cdot r</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> is the correction ratio. This ensures model calls focus on high-dynamics regions while maximizing skips in smooth regions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Error Analysis.</span>
The total approximation error consists of discretization error from numerical integration, prediction error from polynomial extrapolation during skips, and accumulated drift from consecutive skips. Our framework mitigates these by using higher-order AB/AM methods to reduce discretization error, adaptive skip interval to limit prediction error in curved regions, and ABM correction to reset accumulated drift when <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{n}</annotation></semantics></math> exceeds the threshold. Detailed error bounds are provided in <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Error Analysis ‣ Predict to Skip: Linear Multistep Feature Forecasting for Efficient Diffusion Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>, and the complete algorithm is presented in <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Algorithm Pseudocode ‣ Predict to Skip: Linear Multistep Feature Forecasting for Efficient Diffusion Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Experimental Settings</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Models, Datasets, and Solvers.</span>
We evaluate PrediT on three representative DiT-based models. For text-to-image generation, we use FLUX.1-dev <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Labs et al., 2025</a>)</cite> with 50 sampling steps and prompts from DiffusionDB <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. For text-to-video generation, we use HunyuanVideo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kong et al., 2024</a>)</cite> with Rectified Flow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2022b</a>)</cite> solver,
with prompts from VBench gallery <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. For class-to-image generation, we use DiT-XL/2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peebles and Xie, 2023</a>)</cite> with DDIM solver <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al., 2020a</a>)</cite>
on ImageNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2009</a>)</cite> 256<math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>256.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation Metrics.</span>
For text-to-image, we report ImageReward <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2023</a>)</cite> to measure human preference alignment, CLIP Score <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2021</a>)</cite> for text-image consistency, and Aesthetic Score for visual appeal. For text-to-video, we use VBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> for semantic quality and LPIPS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, SSIM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2004</a>)</cite>, PSNR for frame-level fidelity compared to the original output. For class-to-image, we report FID and sFID <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Heusel et al., 2017</a>)</cite> for distribution similarity and Inception Score (IS) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Salimans et al., 2016</a>)</cite> for sample quality and diversity.
Detailed metric definitions are provided in <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Evaluation Metrics ‣ Predict to Skip: Linear Multistep Feature Forecasting for Efficient Diffusion Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Implementation Details.</span>
All experiments are conducted with FlashAttention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dao et al., 2022</a>)</cite> enabled. FLUX. 1 and HunyuanVideo are evaluated on a single NVIDIA A800 80GB GPU, while DiT-XL/2 uses an NVIDIA RTX 4090 24GB GPU. For FLUX.1, we generate 1024<math id="S4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>1024 images. For HunyuanVideo, we test two settings: 544p<math id="S4.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>860p with 17 frames and 480p<math id="S4.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>640p with 45 frames. For DiT-XL/2, we generate 50K 256<math id="S4.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>256 images on ImageNet for FID evaluation. All baselines share the same solver, number of denoising steps, and CFG scale, unless otherwise specified by the original method.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18093v1/flux.png" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:476/670;" width="476" height="670" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S4.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Visual quality comparison of different acceleration methods on FLUX. PrediT achieves higher acceleration while maintaining comparable visual quality.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Text-to-Image Generation</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Quantitative Results.</span>
We evaluate PrediT on FLUX. 1 for text-to-image generation and compare with representative acceleration methods in <a href="#S3.T1" title="In 3.2 PrediT Framework ‣ 3 Method ‣ Predict to Skip: Linear Multistep Feature Forecasting for Efficient Diffusion Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. At comparable acceleration ratios, PrediT matches or improves generation quality across all metrics. Specifically, PrediT achieves superior speedup while attaining the highest ImageReward and CLIP Score, even surpassing the original 50-step baseline. When pushing to more aggressive acceleration, PrediT reaches up to <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="5.54\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5.54</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5.54\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup with only marginal quality degradation. In contrast, reuse-based methods such as <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math>-DiT and FORA suffer from noticeable quality drops at lower speedups. TeaCache achieves only <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2.26\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2.26</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.26\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup but yields a lower ImageReward, significantly below the original. Prediction-based methods like TaylorSeer show improved quality retention but still fall short of PrediT at equivalent accelerations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Visual Comparison.</span>
<a href="#S4.F5" title="In 4.1 Experimental Settings ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Predict to Skip: Linear Multistep Feature Forecasting for Efficient Diffusion Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> presents qualitative comparisons on FLUX. 1 (full prompts are provided in <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Text-to-Image Prompt ‣ Predict to Skip: Linear Multistep Feature Forecasting for Efficient Diffusion Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>, and more visual results are shown in <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F More Visual Results ‣ Predict to Skip: Linear Multistep Feature Forecasting for Efficient Diffusion Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>). Other acceleration methods exhibit visible artifacts including blurriness and loss of fine details, particularly in regions with complex textures. PrediT maintains visual fidelity comparable to the original model while achieving significantly higher acceleration, demonstrating the effectiveness of our principled prediction approach over naive feature reuse.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ablation Study.</span>
To validate the effectiveness of our predictor-corrector scheme and Dynamic Step Modulation (DSM), we conduct ablation experiments on FLUX. 1 as shown in <a href="#S4.T2" title="In 4.2 Text-to-Image Generation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Predict to Skip: Linear Multistep Feature Forecasting for Efficient Diffusion Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. Using only AB predictor without DSM achieves <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3.65\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.65</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.65\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup but with degraded ImageReward. Adding DSM to AB increases speedup to <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="6.49\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>6.49</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">6.49\times</annotation></semantics></math> while maintaining similar quality, demonstrating that adaptive step modulation allows larger skipping in smooth regions. Using ABM alone with DSM yields <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3.86\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.86</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.86\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup with improved quality, showing the benefit of the corrector in high-dynamics regions. The full PrediT framework, which dynamically selects between AB and ABM based on the dynamics metric, achieves an effective balance with <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="4.28\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4.28</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4.28\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup and the highest ImageReward, validating the effectiveness of combining predictive feature forecasting with adaptive step modulation.</p>
</div>

<td id="S4.T3.5.1.17.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E6E6E6;"><span id="S4.T3.5.1.17.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E6E6E6;">80.14</span></td>
